name: Olga Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'll tell you what I think. I'm not shy about it at church either.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brekke and Sons, a family firm out in the countryside that builds farm buildings: barns, cattle sheds, machinery stores, and we repair old farmhouses too. I do the timber framing and the roof sheeting, and sometimes I'm on a farm forty minutes away for a week at a time. I love the big open buildings and the smell of fresh timber in the morning. What wears me out is the mud, the long drives and the cold in February.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Erik, who drives a delivery van for a parcel company, and we rent a little cottage at the edge of the village. I sing in the church choir on Sundays. Money's tight, Brekke pays less than the town firms, and we've got less than a month saved because we just bought a second-hand car. I use an AI chat now and then to check a building rule, but that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So AI stays a small thing. Our farmers won't notice and neither will I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, real work is still real work. I'd tell people in the village that good trades still matter. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, farmers will always need a new barn roof after a bad winter, and the family firm I work for will always need someone to climb up and fix it. The worry is just money, the pay's low and the car ate our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Brekke and put fifty a week aside till we've got two months saved. I'd ask Mr Brekke about a small pay rise in spring, when the barn season starts. And I'd keep using the AI for the odd regulation question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. A little uneasy about money, like most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Brekke when you asked for a rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I've been with him five years and I can frame a barn without being told. I'd say it politely, he's fair if you're respectful. He might say yes in spring, he never says yes in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And how does Erik's work look in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, busy. He's out from six till six, and the parcels never stop. If AI is mostly hype, nothing much changes for him either.

say: She'd say **real work** is still real work after all the fuss.
She'd tell the village that **good trades** still matter, and share **apprenticeship** news.
think: Farmers will always need **barn roofs** fixed, so her job is safe.
Her worry is **low pay** and savings spent on a car.
do: Save **fifty a week** until two months is put aside.
Ask Mr Brekke for a **pay rise** in spring.
Keep using AI for the odd **regulation** question.
S0.quote: Farmers will always need a new barn roof after a bad winter, and the family firm I work for will always need someone to climb up and fix it.
fieldNote: Job feels **secure** in rural farm building, but thin savings keep her **uneasy**.
Respects **family firm** ways: asks for a rise politely, in the right season.
Uses AI **occasionally**, as a steady adopter would.

steps.text: Save fifty a week until two months' costs are put aside
Ask Mr Brekke for a pay rise when barn season starts
Keep checking building rules with an AI chat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the pricing and the paperwork change, and the barns still need hands for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small firms should be free to use whatever tools help them compete. I'd say government shouldn't make it harder with red tape. People who learn and work hard will find a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my boss Mr Brekke has a son who wants an AI program to price our barn jobs, and I'd use it once I'd seen it get three prices right. My hands are fine for now, but I'd worry about Erik's company planning his routes with software and squeezing more drops into his day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let Mr Brekke's son show me the pricing program and use it once I'd seen it work. I'd ask about going on the farm building course at the agricultural college, so I could do the drawings too. And I'd keep saving, maybe less, because Erik might lose his overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why three prices right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first one could be luck, and the second could be the boss's son fiddling it. Three right and I'd trust it. That's how I'd judge a new apprentice too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Erik lost his overtime, what changes at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd skip the holiday and keep the wedding small, which my mum won't like. We'd still pay the rent. Family would help if it came to that, they always have.

say: Small firms should be **free** to use tools that help them **compete**.
Government shouldn't add **red tape**, and hard workers will find a place.
think: She'd trust the **pricing program** after three right answers.
Erik's **delivery routes** could be squeezed by planning software.
do: Learn the **pricing program** from Mr Brekke's son.
Ask about a **farm building course** at the agricultural college.
Keep saving, though less if Erik loses **overtime**.
S1.quote: My boss Mr Brekke has a son who wants an AI program to price our barn jobs, and I'd use it once I'd seen it get three prices right.
fieldNote: Her own work looks safe; Erik's **overtime** is the household risk, so **uneasy**.
Steady adopter with a clear test: **three right prices**.
Free-market view: firms should be **free to compete**.

steps.text: Learn the barn pricing program from Mr Brekke's son
Apply for the farm building drawing course at the agricultural college
Plan a smaller wedding if Erik loses overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So by 2031 there's a robot that can frame a barn. And drive a van, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not the government's job to stop it, but it is everyone's job to look after their own. Families and churches will have to pull together. I'd say that at choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my fiancé Erik drives a delivery van, and a robot that can drive and carry boxes takes his job the same year a robot takes mine. We'd both be out around 2031 with almost nothing saved. Mr Brekke's pricing goes in 2028, but my hands and Erik's driving would follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd ask Mr Brekke if I could learn to run whatever machines he buys, because he'd want someone he trusts. We'd move in with my parents on their farm to save the rent. And we'd bring the wedding forward and keep it tiny, so we're settled before things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want us to face it as a family, not as two people who might split up under the pressure. My parents married in a hard year and they're still together. A small wedding costs less anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen in the three years between AGI and robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd work as hard as we could and save every bit. Farmers would still need barns, and Erik would still be driving. It's like knowing the harvest is the last one.

say: It's not government's job to stop it, but everyone should **look after** their own.
Families and **churches** will have to pull together.
think: Erik's **van job** and her **carpentry** both go around 2031.
Pricing goes in 2028, but **hands-on work** follows soon after.
do: Ask Mr Brekke to train her on any **new machines** he buys.
Move in with her **parents** on their farm to save rent.
Bring the **wedding forward** and keep it tiny.
S2.quote: My fiancé Erik drives a delivery van, and a robot that can drive and carry boxes takes his job the same year a robot takes mine.
fieldNote: Both household incomes gone by 2031 with **almost no savings**: **alarmed**.
Turns to **family, farm and church**, not government.
Sees the three-year gap as a **last harvest** to save from.

steps.text: Ask Mr Brekke to train her on any new building machines
Move in with her parents on their farm to save rent
Bring the wedding forward and keep it small
Save every spare bit of pay before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So 2031, and robots by 2034. More time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for firms to train young people, not for handouts. I'd say families should plan and help each other. I'd say it to anyone who asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to take on an apprentice and teach that young person everything I know, even if the robots come after. And I'd want to get into the drawing and planning side before the barns are robot work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd persuade Mr Brekke to take on an apprentice and offer to train her. I'd do the farm building course in the first year, evenings. Erik and I would start saving for a deposit on a small house near my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's purpose in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: But the drawing and planning side is thinking work that goes in 2031. Why move there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, I hadn't thought of that. Maybe I'd be checking what the computer draws, someone who knows how a barn stands up. I honestly don't know how long that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why train an apprentice if robots are coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because she'd have five good years and a trade to show for it. And because that's how it's always been done, you pass it on. I'd want that to mean something.

say: Firms should **train young people** rather than give **handouts**.
Families should **plan** and help each other through it.
think: Five years is enough to **train an apprentice** properly.
She'd want to move into **drawing and planning** before robots arrive.
do: Persuade Mr Brekke to take on an **apprentice** she'll train.
Do the **farm building course** in the evenings.
Start saving with Erik for a **house deposit**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to take on an apprentice and teach that young person everything I know, even if the robots come after.
fieldNote: More time eases her to **anxious**, but both jobs still end by 2034.
Admits her **planning idea** may not survive AGI.
Passing on the trade matters to her **values**, even short-term.

steps.text: Persuade Mr Brekke to take on an apprentice she trains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and robots in 2039. That's a long time out here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get on with life. Get married, work hard, learn a bit more each year. I'd say the same in this village as I'd say anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, with ten years, I'd rather spend the time building a family and a trade than watching the news about robots. Robots will come to the countryside last, I think, so my barns might last past 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next summer as planned. I'd keep working and do the course over two years, not rushing. And Erik and I would save for a house, and maybe start a family in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little uneasy about Erik's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think robots come to the countryside last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the roads are bad, the farms are far apart and every barn sits on a different slope. A robot that works on a flat city site would hate a muddy hillside. I might be wrong, but that's my guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Erik?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His van would go sooner, I think, the town routes first. He'd have years to plan though. He's talked about working for my dad on the farm one day.

People should **work hard** and learn a bit more each year.
think: Ten years is for building a **family and a trade**.

do: Do the **farm building course** over two years.
Save for a **house** and plan a family.

S4.quote: With ten years, I'd rather spend the time building a family and a trade than watching the news about robots.
fieldNote: A decade plus rural work makes her own income feel **safe**: **uneasy**.
Reasons that **muddy, scattered farms** slow robots down.
Erik may move to her father's **farm**: family as fallback.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Erik and I would both lose our work in the same year with nothing saved. What would help is firms getting support to take on apprentices for the new jobs, and families being able to lean on each other without the rules getting in the way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the countryside. A family firm out in the countryside will be the last place a robot turns up, but it will turn up.

headlineQuote: A family firm out in the countryside will be the last place a robot turns up, but it will turn up.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old carpenter** building barns and farm sheds for a rural family firm.
She's engaged to Erik, a **delivery van driver**, and they have under a month saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** and trusts new tools once she's seen them work.
She believes in **family, church and apprenticeships** more than government help.
Her mood is **uneasy** in slower pictures and **alarmed** when both jobs end by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Erik would lose their work in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: Support for firms to take on **apprentices** in new jobs.
Letting **families** lean on each other without rules getting in the way.
